name: IBO Nurture A3 - The $26M difference
subject: The $26M difference
preview: Same company, same value, two outcomes.
html:
{{ personalization_token('contact.firstname', 'there') }}, one number explains why owners look at this.

 

Take a company worth $50M. Sold to a PE firm, after federal and state capital gains the owner typically nets about $37.8M, plus a required earnout and rollover and a board that now outvotes them.

 

The same company, at the same $50M, structured as an Independent Buyout (IBO), nets about $64.2M: the sale proceeds are tax-free, and the owner keeps warrants on the future upside and keeps running the business.

 

That's $26.4M difference on the same enterprise value. The full comparison, line by line, is here: www.iboadvisors.com/blog/ibo-vs-pe-numbers-comparison

 

Worth 20 minutes to learn about an Independent Buyout (IBO) and run your numbers?

name: IBO Nurture A4 - The Founders/Owners Exit Conversation is Broken
subject: The Founders/Owners Exit Conversation is Broken
preview: The Exit Conversation is Broken.
html:
{{ personalization_token('contact.firstname', 'there') }},

 

Here's what nobody in the advisory world will say out loud: The exit conversation in America is broken - and it's broken on purpose.

 

If you own a profitable business doing $3M+ in EBITDA, your options have been framed for you by people who get paid when you pick one of two doors: (1) Sell to Private Equity, or (2) Sell to a Competitor.

 

What if you could do the same type of transaction that Private Equity does when buying your company - but without the Private Equity? This isn't theoretical. It's called an Independent Buyout (IBO).

 

The reason you haven't heard about it is the same reason the menu only has two doors: nobody in your current advisory circle gets paid to show you Door 3.

name: IBO Nurture B2 - The four levers that move EBITDA
subject: The four levers that move EBITDA
preview: Most $1M-$3M companies are closer to $3M than the P&L says.
html:
{{ personalization_token('contact.firstname', 'there') }},

 

Most companies in the $1M-$3M range are closer to $3M than their P&L says. Four things buyers will add back or reprice, and that you can move on purpose:

 

1. Owner compensation above market rate.
2. One-off costs: litigation, a bad hire, a system migration.
3. Pricing that hasn't kept pace with your costs.
4. Product or customer mix: the low-margin work that fills the schedule.

 

If you do these things and your EBITDA lands you above $3M, reply and we'll talk.

 

Best,

Edmund Breitling

Partner, IBO Advisors
